doc_summary: The paper compares MNLI-style crowdworker-written entailment data against two fully automatic pair-generation protocols under a fixed annotation budget, finding the automatic protocols clearly worse on NLI generalization and transfer. It concludes that human writing remains the best known option and that effort should go into improving it.

items.claim: prefers comparing a new method against a strong, faithfully replicated baseline under matched resource constraints over reporting the new method in isolation, because only then does a result show whether the method is actually better.
items.quote: To study the cost trade-off, we collect each dataset under the same fixed annotation budget with a fixed ($\sim$ US \$15) hourly wage. Using this constraint, we collect approximately twice as many examples from our new protocols.

items.claim: Checks that the pipeline is sound by confirming the baseline reproduces known behavior (Base should resemble MNLI) before trusting the comparisons against it.
items.quote: Overall, our Base shows better transfer learning performance compared to MNLI, suggesting that our setup is sound. However, we also see that our new protocols perform worse than Base, showing that they produce less useful training data than the strong baseline of crowdworker writing.

items.claim: Distrusts results from tiny evaluation sets and refuses to draw conclusions from them.
items.quote: We also see some positive transfer for COPA, however since its validation set is very small (100 examples), we can not conclude anything with confidence.

items.claim: Distrusts human-written data because writing introduces artifacts that models exploit via spurious statistical patterns, so a benchmark's apparent performance may not reflect the intended capability.
items.quote: there is growing evidence that human writing can introduce annotation artifacts, which enable models to perform moderately well just by learning spurious statistical patterns in the data

items.claim: Uses multiple diagnostic probes (hypothesis-only models, PMI word-label associations, lexical overlap, qualitative inspection) to detect artifacts rather than relying on one headline metric.
items.quote: We find that word type overlap is a much stronger predictor of the label in our new protocols than in Base. This could be a significant driver of our results and might hurt the generalization performance

items.claim: prefers evaluating on downstream transfer and cross-dataset generalization over in-distribution scores because in-distribution results can be inflated by shared artifacts.
items.quote: Our new protocols show lower performance than the Base, but that may just be because they are of lower overall quality and not because they are less solvable by the hypothesis-only models. We verify this by looking at their transfer learning performance

items.claim: prefers reporting clear negative results with honest framing over spinning a mixed outcome, because they redirect the field's effort.
items.quote: Our main results on natural language inference and transfer learning are clearly negative. Human-constructed examples appear to be far superior to automatically-constructed examples in both settings.

items.claim: Abandons a direction after serious effort (state-of-the-art tools, piloting, tuning) yields negative results, while explicitly noting what was not exhausted.
items.quote: given that we use state-of-the-art tools including FAISS, RoBERTa, and OPUS, and refine our methods with several rounds of piloting and tuning, we are skeptical that there is low-hanging fruit in the two directions we explored.

items.claim: Proposes future work on improving crowdworker writing processes rather than replacing human writing.
items.quote: Future work along this line might focus on crowdsourcing strategies (beyond the basic HIT design) which encourage crowdworkers to produce high-quality data with reduced artifacts.

items.claim: Wary of synthetic LLM-generated data as a source of hard-to-diagnose bias, since it still depends on human-written data.
items.quote: this would still require training data from crowdworker-written dataset, and might add a major source of potentially difficult-to-diagnose bias.
